pages.text: Mr Konney stopped the class at the gate of Cape Coast Castle. “This is a serious place,” he said. “Some of what we hear today is sad. We will walk quietly and listen. If anyone needs a moment, step outside and tell me. There is no shame in that.” Tawia nodded. Rosina held her notebook close.

There is no shame in that.” Tawia nodded.

pages.text: “This place began as a Portuguese trading post in 1555,” said Mr Konney. “Later, a Swedish company built a wooden lodge here and named it Carolusborg, for King Charles X. Books give the year as 1652 or 1653. The Dutch took over, and in 1664 the English captured it and called it Cape Coast Castle.”

“Later, a Swedish company built a wooden lodge here and named it Carolusborg, for King Charles X.
Books give the year as 1652 or 1653.
The Dutch took over, and in 1664 the English captured it and called it Cape Coast Castle.”
pages.alt: A timeline with a small wooden lodge, a Dutch flag and an English flag.

pages.text: “For many years, one of the main trades here was in enslaved people,” said Mr Konney. “Captured men, women and children were held in this castle until ships came to take them across the Atlantic. Below us is a dungeon. One source says it was built by 1682 and could hold about a thousand people. Historians are not sure of the date, and the number is an estimate.”

pages.alt: A staircase leading down into a dim stone room, drawn without any people in it.

pages.text: The guide led them to a narrow doorway that opened toward the sea. “This is called the Door of No Return,” he said quietly. “It was the last step before the ships.” Nobody spoke. Rosina looked at the sea beyond the door, blue and wide and very quiet.

“It was the last step before the ships.” Nobody spoke.
Rosina looked at the sea beyond the door, blue and wide and very quiet.
pages.alt: A narrow stone doorway with the sea and sky visible beyond it.

pages.text: “Notice the words we use,” said Mr Konney. “We say enslaved people, not slaves. Those who were held here were not defined by what was done to them. They were human beings with names, families, farms, songs and skills. Using the right words reminds us of that.” Tawia crossed out a word in his notebook and wrote it again.

pages.text: “After the trade ended, the castle was kept and mended over the years,” said Mr Konney. “The British Public Works Department repaired it in the 1920s. In 1957 it passed to the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board. It was restored again in the early 1990s with help from the Ghanaian government and international partners. UNESCO listed it in 1979 with other forts and castles on our coast.”

UNESCO listed it in 1979 with other forts and castles on our coast.”
pages.alt: Workers repair a stone wall with scaffolding beside a white castle.

pages.text: “Why do we not knock it down?” asked Rosina. Mr Konney thought for a while. “Because forgetting does not heal anything,” he said. “A place like this lets us tell the truth, honour the people who suffered, and teach children who were not there. Many visitors come simply to stand in silence and remember.”

pages.alt: Pupils stand quietly in a courtyard while the teacher answers a question.

pages.text: On the way out, they passed through the same doorway. “Some people now also speak of a Door of Return,” said the guide, “to welcome the descendants of those who were taken, and to say: you are not forgotten.” Tawia and Rosina stepped out into the sunshine together. For a long time neither of them said anything. The end.
